# A bounded denominator for externally translated radicals over fields with few roots of unity

<a id="statement"></a>
## The field generated by the original number

Let \(\beta\in\overline{\mathbf Q}^{\times}\) be nontorsion and \(F=\mathbf Q(\beta)\).
Write \(\mu(F)\) for the roots of unity in \(F\) and \(w=|\mu(F)|\).
Let \(k_F\) be the largest positive integer \(k\) for which \(\theta^k=\epsilon\beta\) for some \(\theta\in F^\times\) and \(\epsilon\in\mu(F)\).
Write \(m(\beta)=[F:\mathbf Q]h(\beta)\), with \(h\) the absolute logarithmic Weil height.
For any \(g\ge1\) range over every root of unity \(\eta\) and every solution \(\alpha^g=\eta\beta\).
In particular \(\eta\) may lie outside \(F\).

If \(\mu(F)=\{1,-1\}\), all such ratios \(m(\alpha)/m(\beta)\) are positive integral multiples of \(1/\gcd(g,k_F)\), and this smallest value occurs.
If additionally \(\beta\) is annihilated by a nonzero integer polynomial of coefficient length at most \(L\), then
\[
          k_F\mid R_L,\qquad
          \frac{m(\alpha)}{m(\beta)}
               \in\frac{1}{\gcd(g,R_L)}\mathbf Z_{>0},                  \tag{1}
\]
where \(R_L\) is the [bounded-length denominator for ordinary radicals](Yin_C_G0345_v210.md#statement).
This includes all fields with a real embedding and also totally imaginary fields with only the two rational roots of unity.
In a real embedding the positive root \(|\beta|^{1/g}\) attains the minimum.

For general \(F\) one has
\[
          m(\alpha)\ge
             \frac{m(\beta)}{\varphi(w)\gcd(g,k_F)}.                    \tag{2}
\]
In particular, for any nontorsion algebraic unit \(\beta\) of coefficient length at most \(L\) in the preceding sense,
\[
          m(\alpha)\ge \frac{m(\beta)}{H_L w\varphi(w)},                 \tag{3}
\]
where \(H_L\) is the [arbitrary-phase saturation bound](Yin_C_G0345_v767.md#statement).
Thus if such seeds have \(m(\beta)\ge c>0\) and some translated radicals have \(m(\alpha)\to0\), then \(w\to\infty\), regardless of the number of seed conjugates which differ by roots of unity.
For a nonunit the same shrinking scenario is excluded by \(m(\alpha)\ge\log2\), since it too is a nonunit.
A positive lower bound for \(m(\beta)\) for arbitrary bounded-length units remains open.

<a id="prior"></a>
## The known minimum in terms of the minimal field

Write \([x]\) for the class of \(x\) in the rational vector space \(\overline{\mathbf Q}^{\times}/\mu(\overline{\mathbf Q})\), in additive notation, and put \(f=[\beta]\).
The [degree theorem of Fili and Miner](../audits/literature/FM13/Yin_U002.md#rational-line-degree) already gives the minimum degree of every rational multiple of \(f\) over all its torsion representatives.
We use its parameters in order to compare that minimum with the degree and divisibility in the original field \(F\).

Let \(K=K_f\) denote the minimal field in that theorem, and put \(\delta=[K:\mathbf Q]\) and \(\kappa=[F:K]\).
One may obtain \(K\) as \(\mathbf Q(\beta^B)\) by taking \(B\) divisible by all orders of quotients of conjugates by \(\beta\) that are roots of unity.
The field \(K\) is contained in the field generated by every representative of any nonzero rational multiple of \(f\).
In \(K^\times/\mu(K)\), choose \(u\in K^\times\) representing the positive generator of its intersection with the oriented rational line \(\mathbf Q f\).
There are coprime positive integers \(a,b\) with \(b f=a[u]\).
Thus \(b/a\) generates the rational multiples of \(f\) represented in \(K\).
Likewise the rational multiples of \(f\) represented in \(F\) form \((1/k_F)\mathbf Z\).
Indeed this subgroup contains \(1\) and meets each bounded real interval in a finite set by Northcott's theorem on representatives of bounded height in the fixed field \(F\).
This proves the existence of \(k_F\) for units and nonunits alike.

For \(g\ge1\) put \(\lambda=\gcd(a,g)\), \(p=a/\lambda\) and \(q=bg/\lambda\), so \([ \alpha]=(p/q)[u]\) in lowest terms.
For any representative \(\alpha\) put \(t=[\mathbf Q(\alpha):K]\).
Its conjugates over \(K\) have the same class, because \([u]\) is fixed and the quotient by torsion is a rational vector space.
The norm to \(K\) therefore represents \((tp/q)[u]\), which implies \(q\mid t\) by the choice of \(u\).
Conversely a root of \(X^q-u^p\) represents this class, generates a field containing \(K\), and has degree at most \(q\) over \(K\).
It attains the bound.
This is exactly the relative norm mechanism of Fili and Miner's Proposition 3.2.
Taking \(g=1\) at the given representative \(\beta\) yields \(b\mid\kappa\).
Set \(e=\kappa/b\).
Since \(h(\alpha)=h(\beta)/g\), the ratios \(m(\alpha)/m(\beta)\) are positive integral multiples of \(1/(e\gcd(g,a))\), and that minimum occurs.

<a id="comparison"></a>
## Comparing the two fields using the roots of unity in the original one

There is a root of unity \(\xi=\beta^b/u^a\in F\).
Over \(K(\xi)\) the polynomial \(X^b-\xi u^a\) annihilates \(\beta\).
Since \(K(\xi)\subset F=\mathbf Q(\beta)\), it follows that
\[
                   1\le e\le [K(\xi):K]\le\varphi(w).                  \tag{4}
\]
The integers \(a,b\) being coprime, choose \(i,j\in\mathbf Z\) with \(ia+jb=1\).
The class of \(\beta^iu^j\in F^\times\) is \([u]/b=f/a\).
Consequently \(a\mid k_F\).
Conversely there is \(\theta\in F^\times\) with \([\theta]=f/k_F\).
All \(F\)-embeddings over \(K\) preserve that class, since it is a rational multiple of \([u]\).
Their product represents \(\kappa f/k_F=(ae/k_F)[u]\) in \(K\), forcing \(k_F\mid ae\).
In particular
\[
                           a\mid k_F\mid ae.                             \tag{5}
\]
Equations (4) and (5) give (2), and the unit bound \(k_F\le H_Lw\) from the [saturation theorem](Yin_C_G0345_v767.md#statement) gives (3).
These estimates control the effect of the original field's torsion even when \(\kappa\) grows without bound.

More precisely, whenever \(\mu(F)\subset K\), (4) gives \(e=1\) and (5) gives \(a=k_F\).
This holds in particular if \(\mu(F)=\{1,-1\}\).
In that case an element realizing \(k_F\) satisfies \(\theta^{k_F}=\pm\beta\), and \(\mathbf Q(\theta)=F\) because \(\theta\in F\) and this power generates \(F\).
The seed \(\pm\beta\) is annihilated by \(P(\pm X)\) with the same coefficient length.
The ordinary denominator theorem with relative degree one gives \(k_F\mid R_L\), proving (1).

<a id="real"></a>
## A positive minimizing radical in a real embedding

Work in a chosen real embedding of \(F\) and extend it to the algebraic closure.
For any real nonzero algebraic number \(y\) and any root of unity \(\zeta\) of order \(n\), the degree of \(y\) divides the degree of \(\zeta y\).
Indeed \(K'=\mathbf Q(y^n)\) is a real subfield of both fields.
The norm from either field to \(K'\) equals \(y^t\) times a root of unity, where \(t\) is its degree over \(K'\), since all relevant conjugates have \(n\)-th power \(y^n\).
That root of unity is real and hence is a sign.
The least positive exponent \(s\) with \(y^s\in K'\) divides both degrees \(t\).
The relative degree for \(y\) is also at most \(s\), so it equals \(s\).
Now \(\gamma=|\beta|^{1/g}\) represents \(f/g\) and every other representative is \(\zeta\gamma\).
Their heights agree and \(\gamma\) realizes the minimum.

The original degree can decrease under an external phase if the field has more torsion.
For example let \(u=(1+\sqrt5)/2\), let \(\zeta\) have order three, and put \(\beta=\zeta u\).
Since \(\beta^3=2u+1\), its field is \(\mathbf Q(u,\zeta)\) of degree four.
The polynomial \(X^4+X^3+2X^2-X+1\) annihilates \(\beta\), so its coefficient length is six.
At \(g=1\), the allowed representative \(u=\zeta^{-1}\beta\) has degree two and \(m(u)=m(\beta)/2\).
This demonstrates the need to account for additional torsion even at a fixed coefficient length.
